claims.chapter: Ch. XVII: On the Theory of Transformations, or the Comparison of Related Forms
claims.label: Parahippus is a divergent offshoot, not on the direct line to Equus
claims.statement: Because the skull of Parahippus fits the interpolated transformation series from Eohippus to Equus poorly, Parahippus is not in the direct line of descent but represents a divergent branch of the Equidae.

operationalizations.text: Test Parahippus placement using public morphological and molecularly calibrated total-evidence equid phylogenies, independently of its fit to a skull transformation. Topological support for or against direct ancestry resolves the historical inference.

Place Parahippus on the same Hyracotherium-to-Equus morph and on a cladogram of equids built from characters other than the interpolated skull warp. The claim is supported if Parahippus is both a poor geometric fit and sits off the Equus stem; a good fit, or a stem position despite a poor fit, would separate the geometric evidence from the phylogenetic conclusion.

obstacles: Direct ancestry is harder to establish than sister-group placement.
Fossil character matrices contain missing data.
A poor fit to a linear warp can reflect age, sex or crushing rather than a side branch.
Equid phylogeny is morphological, so the tree and the skull transformation share character evidence.

Occurrence and taxonomic context for Parahippus and the other equid genera in the comparison

claims.chapter: Ch. XV: On the Shapes of Eggs, and of Certain Other Hollow Structures
claims.label: The most pointed eggs are those largest relative to the parent bird
claims.statement: As a very common rule, the most asymmetrical, posteriorly tapered eggs are those that are large relative to the parent bird (guillemot, curlews, sandpipers, terns), because they are under the greatest pressure in the oviduct; relatively large but symmetrical eggs (apteryx) imply a relatively large oviduct.

operationalizations.text: Across bird species, relate quantitative egg asymmetry and posterior taper to egg volume divided by adult female body size, controlling phylogeny and ecology. A robust positive association supports the empirical rule; no association refutes it, while direct oviduct dimensions would be needed for the pressure explanation.

Regress egg asymmetry on egg size relative to adult body size across species, with a phylogenetic control, and inspect named cases such as guillemots, sandpipers, terns, and Apteryx. The common rule is supported by a positive relationship and by the stated exceptions having large oviducts; the pressure explanation is not tested unless oviduct pressure, rather than relative size alone, is measured.

obstacles: Oviduct size and in vivo pressure are generally absent.
Phylogeny, flight ecology and clutch strategy confound the association.
Relative size is a proxy for the pressure Thompson invokes, and flight or nesting correlates can produce the same pattern.
Oviduct dimensions in the open file are not pressure records along the forming egg.

roles: Public species-level body mass and reproductive trait data for relative egg-size calculations.

roles: Species-level egg shape together with oviduct and pelvic measurements for a large sample of birds

roles: Public egg specimen images and taxonomic metadata.

claims.chapter: Ch. XIII: The Shapes of Horns, and of Teeth or Tusks: with a Note on Torsion
claims.label: The thicker the horn, the greater its spiral curvature
claims.statement: On the whole, thicker horns are more strongly spirally curved than slender ones, because a larger cross-section allows greater differences in growth or retardation between opposite sides.

operationalizations.text: Across species of Bovidae (antelopes, goats, sheep), regress mean spiral curvature (normalized by horn length or basal radius) against basal horn cross-sectional thickness/diameter using 3D cranial scans and comparative morphometric datasets.

Measure horn cross-sectional thickness and centerline curvature in a taxonomically broad 3D sample, then model their association with controls for body size, sex, age and phylogeny. A robust positive effect supports the claim; a null or negative effect with adequate power refutes it.

Regress a curvature or spiral-tightness measure on basal horn diameter across antelopes, goats, and sheep, with a phylogenetic control. The claim is supported by a positive thickness–curvature relationship within and across clades; no relationship, or the reverse, would refute the stated tendency.

obstacles: Curvature has units of inverse length, so the correlation depends on whether raw curvature, radius of curvature, or spiral angle (dimensionless) is tested against horn thickness.
Thickness and curvature both covary with body size and age.
External scans may not reveal sheath thickness separately from the core.
Related species share both thick horns and strong spirals, so a naive correlation is phylogenetically confounded.
Scanned samples under-represent slender-horned antelopes relative to sheep and goats.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
roles: Provides 3D scans of bovid horns across a wide range of basal thicknesses and curvatures.
3D specimens for measuring horn thickness and curvature.
3D bovid skulls from which basal diameter and centerline curvature can be measured together

candidate_datasets.name: iDigBio
roles: Public bovid specimen images and metadata to broaden taxonomic coverage.
Additional specimens to widen the sample of slender and heavy horns

claims.label: Cephalopod septa take the form of minimal surfaces like soap films
claims.statement: Because a septum is first laid down as an elastic membrane under uniform pressure, it takes the shape of a soap film with the same boundary, a surface of minimal area: spherical in a straight cone with a perpendicular attachment, ellipsoidal with an oblique attachment, and saddle-shaped where the line of attachment is sinuous.

operationalizations.text: Extract septal surfaces and attachment boundaries from 3D shells, solve the corresponding minimal-surface problem, and compare observed curvature and area with minimal, constant-mean-curvature and biomechanical alternatives. Shape classes should track boundary orientation as predicted.

From CT of nautiloid and ammonoid septa, estimate mean curvature given the suture as boundary, and compare spherical, ellipsoidal and saddle cases with the attachment Thompson describes. Near-zero mean curvature supports a minimal surface; systematic mean curvature, or a better fit by a non-minimal shell, refutes it.

obstacles: Uniform pressure and isotropic membrane assumptions are not directly recorded.
Fossil deformation and later calcification can alter original septal shape.
Downloadable CT is richer for Nautilus and a few ammonoids than for the full range of orthocones and suture types.
A thin elastic membrane under pressure is minimal only under the isotropy and uniform-pressure assumptions.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
roles: Open micro-CT shell volumes reveal internal cephalopod septa and attachment lines.
Micro-CT of chambered cephalopod shells from which septal surfaces and their boundaries can be meshed.

candidate_datasets.name: Digital Atlas of Ancient Life
roles: Suture outlines and sectioned shells used to classify attachment geometry where full septal scans are lacking.

claims.chapter: Ch. XIII: The Shapes of Horns, and of Teeth or Tusks: with a Note on Torsion
claims.label: Elephant and American mastodon tusks are the same spiral as the mammoth's, only shorter
claims.statement: The tusks of living elephants and American mastodons follow essentially the same logarithmic spiral as the mammoth's great spiral tusks and differ only in size, so that if they grew long enough they would become equally spiral.

operationalizations.text: Fit scale-normalized logarithmic spiral parameters to complete tusk centerlines of living elephants, American mastodons and mammoths, and extrapolate shorter curves with uncertainty. Shared parameters support size-only difference; significant taxon-specific curvature or torsion refutes it.

Fit one logarithmic spiral to complete tusks of mammoths, living elephants, and American mastodons, allowing only a scale difference. The claim is confirmed if a shared angle fits all three once size is removed; species differences in angle, or a scale-free shape difference in pitch or taper, would refute 'the same spiral, only shorter.'

obstacles: Many fossil tusks are incomplete or deformed.
Sex, age and species produce substantial within-group variation.
Complete tusks are heavy, often broken, and less often scanned than the skulls that held them.
A short arc from a living elephant underdetermines the spiral angle that a long mammoth tusk displays.

claims.chapter: Ch. XVI: On Form and Mechanical Efficiency
claims.label: Mechanically shaped single bones are unreliable guides to phylogenetic affinity
claims.statement: Because the form of bones such as the scapula or vertebrae reflects the mechanical stresses of an animal's mode of life, resemblance or difference in a single such bone is no reliable evidence for or against blood-relationship, as in comparing Zeuglodon with whales.

operationalizations.text: Compare phylogenetic accuracy from single mechanically responsive bones against multi-character morphology and molecular reference trees, stratified by ecological convergence. Reliability is measured by topology error and support.

Using molecular or other independent trees as the reference, compare phylogenetic signal and homoplasy of scapulae and vertebrae with that of other skeletal characters, especially in lineages that changed habitat. The claim is supported if those mechanically loaded bones mislead more often than other characters; equal or higher reliability would refute it.

obstacles: Choice of a “mechanically shaped” character may be partly outcome-dependent.
Fossil taxa lack molecular reference trees.
Extinct test cases such as Zeuglodon have no genome, so the reference tree is itself partly morphological.
Character coding and missing fossils change apparent homoplasy.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
roles: Public morphological matrices and phylogenetic projects.
Published morphological matrices containing scapular, vertebral and other skeletal characters

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
roles: Public synthesis trees for independent relationship benchmarks.
Synthetic phylogeny as an independent reference against which skeletal characters can be scored

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
roles: Scans of scapulae and vertebrae for measuring shape convergence among animals with similar habits

claims.chapter: Ch. X: A Parenthetic Note on Geodetics
claims.label: Small swimmers rotate about their axis, turning a constant swerve into a helical path
claims.statement: Small ciliated and flagellated organisms cannot steer, but by rotating about their long axis while swimming they convert a constant body-fixed swerve into a continually changing direction in space, so they travel along a helix around a nearly straight axis rather than in a circle.

operationalizations.text: Track 3D position and body orientation of swimming microorganisms, estimating axial rotation, body-fixed curvature and helix pitch. The mechanism is supported when observed trajectories follow parameters predicted from rotation and swerve and become circular when rotation approaches zero.

From 3D tracks, measure body rotation, path curvature and whether the trajectory is a helix about a nearly straight axis rather than a circle. A helix whose turning matches axial rotation supports the swerve-averaging account; circular paths without rotation, or helices produced without body rotation, refute it for that swimmer.

obstacles: Many videos are two-dimensional.
Phototaxis, boundaries and fluid flow can perturb paths.
The clearest open 3D tracks are bacteria, whereas the claim centers on ciliates, flagellates, rotifers and swarm-spores.
A helical flagellar beat can draw a helix without a constant body-fixed swerve.

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
roles: Cell-motility imaging that can supply tracks for additional flagellates and ciliates where deposited.

candidate_datasets.name: BioStudies
roles: Public supplementary microscopy videos can provide organism trajectories and body orientation.

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad bilophotrichous bacterial tracks
roles: Open 3D swimming trajectories that include helical paths, for a bacterial subset of small swimmers.

claims.chapter: Ch. XVII: On the Theory of Transformations, or the Comparison of Related Forms
claims.label: Fossil horse skulls match interpolated stages between Hyracotherium and Equus
claims.statement: Skulls interpolated by coordinate transformation between Hyracotherium (Eohippus) and Equus coincide closely with actual fossil skulls of Mesohippus and Protohippus, which therefore lie on the transformation series from Eohippus to the horse.

operationalizations.text: Fit a prespecified transformation between Hyracotherium and Equus skulls, generate interpolated surfaces, and measure their blinded geometric distance to Mesohippus and Protohippus versus other equid fossils and null morphospaces.

Build a coordinate path from Hyracotherium to Equus and measure the distance of Mesohippus and Protohippus skulls to the interpolated shapes, relative to skulls that are not on that path. Close coincidence, closer than off-path equids, would support the claim; distances as large as those of unrelated perissodactyls would refute it.

obstacles: Fossil completeness and deformation vary.
Interpolation can be tuned unless fixed before examining intermediates.
Complete, undistorted skulls of the named fossil genera are few, and only some are openly scanned.
A linear morph between two endpoints can pass near intermediate fossils without those fossils lying on the phylogenetic path.

roles: Public fossil and living equid skull scans.
Scans of fossil and living equid skulls where museums have deposited them

Taxonomic and occurrence framework for which equid skulls exist to be measured

claims.chapter: Ch. XVI: On Form and Mechanical Efficiency
claims.label: Quadrupeds carry more of their weight on the fore-legs than on the hind-legs
claims.statement: In large quadrupeds the fore-legs carry considerably more of the body weight than the hind-legs (about 55–58% in horses and elephants and about two-thirds in camels and llamas).

operationalizations.text: Calculate forelimb share of total vertical ground-reaction force during quiet stance in large quadrupeds and test the stated species-specific percentages and general forelimb excess.

Sum vertical ground reactions on the forefeet and hindfeet of standing or slowly walking horses, elephants, camels and llamas and express the fore share of body weight. The claim is confirmed if horses and elephants fall near 55-58 percent and camels and llamas near two-thirds; shares near one-half, or a reversed ranking of those species, would refute the stated figures.

obstacles: Force-plate data for elephants, camels and llamas are limited.
Load distribution changes with posture and movement.
The deposited horse series is a ridden gallop, whereas Thompson's percentages are for the standing load distribution.
Elephant, camel and llama force-plate tables are scattered in papers rather than one open archive.

roles: Open force-plate records giving forelimb versus hindlimb vertical impulse in Thoroughbreds during gallop

claims.chapter: Ch. XIV: On Leaf-Arrangement, or Phyllotaxis
claims.label: Close approximations to the golden mean are rare; poor ones like 2/3 are common
claims.statement: Against the 'ideal angle' theory, phyllotactic arrangements that closely approximate the golden mean (8/13, 13/21, 34/55 and higher) are comparatively rare, while poorer approximations such as 3/5, 2/3 and 1/2 are extremely common.

operationalizations.text: Compile divergence fractions or parastichy ratios from a taxonomically stratified plant sample and compare prevalence of the listed close and poor approximations. Higher frequencies of 1/2, 2/3 and 3/5 than 8/13 and above support the claim; opposite frequencies refute it.

Tabulate phyllotactic fractions across leaves, cones, and capitula and compare the frequency of 1/2, 2/3, and 3/5 with that of 8/13, 13/21, and higher Fibonacci approximations. The claim is supported if the coarser fractions dominate the flora; it is refuted if close approximations are the common case outside large capitula.

obstacles: Image-based samples overrepresent large, conspicuous reproductive structures.
Ratios are not routinely encoded and require extensive annotation.
Sunflowers are enriched for the high pairs the claim says are rare, so that file alone cannot represent phyllotaxis across plants.
Leaf-arrangement surveys remain in botanical compilations rather than one open trait table.

roles: Public specimen imagery from which phyllotactic ratios can be scored.

claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates (continued)
claims.label: Stomata lie in rows on oblong-celled leaves and scattered on polygonal-celled ones
claims.statement: Because the stomatal mother cell is cut off by a minimal partition whose form depends on epidermal cell shape, stomata are arranged in regular rows where epidermal cells are oblong (as in hyacinth) and irregularly where they are polygonal (as in Sedum).

operationalizations.text: Across leaf epidermal images, quantify cell elongation and stomatal row order, testing whether oblong-cell tissues show stronger row alignment than polygonal-cell tissues and whether minimal partitions mediate the relation.

Measure epidermal cell aspect ratio and the spatial arrangement of stomata on the same leaves. Stomata in rows where cells are oblong, and irregularly placed where cells are polygonal, including within lineages that break the monocot-dicot pairing, would support the claim.

obstacles: Open images are not evenly sampled across monocots and dicots.
Venation and developmental patterning can independently impose rows.
The open coordinate table is Arabidopsis, a polygonal case, and does not include the oblong-celled monocot leaves that should show rows.
Monocots tend to have both oblong cells and stomatal files, so phylogeny and cell shape have to be separated.

candidate_datasets.name: Arabidopsis stomatal coordinates
roles: Pixel coordinates of every stomate on 66 Arabidopsis leaves, for testing whether stomata on a polygonal epidermis are scattered rather than rowed

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
roles: Public plant microscopy for epidermal-cell and stomatal spatial analysis.

candidate_datasets.name: TRY Plant Trait Database

claims.label: The same spiral shell forms recur across unrelated groups, all ages and all seas
claims.statement: Spiral shell forms appear with little relation to the kind of animal producing them, recurring in gastropods, cephalopods, foraminifera and tube worms, and mathematically identical forms recur in every geological period and are found mixed together regardless of climate or local conditions.

operationalizations.text: Parameterize spiral shell form across molluscs, foraminifera and tube worms, then model recurrence and convergence against phylogeny, geological age, climate, depth and geography. The claim predicts frequent cross-group near-identity and weak environmental or temporal structure.

Place gastropod, cephalopod, foraminiferal and tube-worm shells in one coiling morphospace and test recurrence of the same forms across clades, geological periods and climate or depth settings. Repeated overlap, with forms mixed within deposits, supports the claim; forms restricted to clade, era or climate refute the corresponding part.

obstacles: Morphology and occurrence databases require substantial taxonomic linkage.
Preservation and collecting biases vary strongly through time and habitat.
Claims about 'every' period and sea exceed actual coverage.
A common measurement protocol for molluscs, foraminifera and worm tubes is not already computed, and worm tubes are sparsely scanned.
Preservation and sampling differ by period and climate, which can create false recurrences or hide real habitat limits.

roles: Open 3D shell forms for quantitative similarity analysis.
3D shells for mathematical comparison of coiling across groups, strongest for molluscs.
